title: From CompTek to Yandex to Nebius
body:
## The CompTek seed

The entity that would eventually become Nebius Group N.V. had its earliest origins not in a search algorithm but in a computer-hardware distribution business. In 1990, John Boynton co-founded CompTek International in Moscow — one of the first generation of commercially oriented technology companies to emerge from the collapsing Soviet system. CompTek's role in the subsequent decade was less that of a technology developer than a corporate nursery: it provided the infrastructure, early capital, and operational scaffolding within which Arkady Volozh and his collaborators built and incubated what would become Russia's dominant internet search engine.

Yandex as a named search product launched in 1997, and the company was formally incorporated in 2000. The ownership and board connections forged in the CompTek incubator persisted directly into the incorporated Yandex entity. Boynton joined the Yandex board at inception in 2000 and did not leave it — serving through every phase of the company's subsequent history and assuming the chairmanship in 2016. His tenure represents the longest unbroken thread of institutional memory in what is now the Nebius Group governance structure.

The second foundational financial connection was forged in 1998, when Charles Ryan — then co-founder and chief executive of United Financial Group, one of the leading Russia-focused investment banks of the post-Soviet era — sponsored an early-stage technology investment through ru-Net Holdings that included Yandex. Ryan had previously led the St. Petersburg privatisation programme for the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development; UFG would later be acquired in its entirety by Deutsche Bank, with Ryan serving as Deutsche Bank Group's chief country officer and CEO for Russia from 2005 to 2008. He joined the Yandex board at the 2011 NASDAQ IPO and remained a director through the full arc of the company's subsequent transformation.

## The dominant decade and the 2022 break

Yandex's 2011 NASDAQ IPO raised approximately $1.3 billion and valued the company at roughly $8 billion, at the time one of the largest internet IPOs since Google. The listing reflected a business that by 2011 controlled more than sixty per cent of Russian internet search — a market-share position it held, and in some periods extended, through the following decade. The 2010s saw Yandex diversify aggressively beyond search: ride-hailing through Yandex.Taxi (a joint venture with Uber that eventually became Yandex.Go), food delivery through Yandex.Eats, cloud infrastructure, self-driving technology through Yandex Self-Driving Group, and the broader ecosystem of verticals that characterised the dominant internet platform model of the era. By the early 2020s Yandex was the most complete Russian-language internet ecosystem in existence, with a NASDAQ-listed equity that gave Western institutional capital indirect exposure to Russian consumer internet growth.

Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine ended that proposition. The political and sanctions pressures that followed created an impossible position for a company incorporated in the Netherlands, listed in New York, and operationally headquartered in Moscow. Volozh stepped down as chief executive in June 2022 — a resignation that he later described, in the context of his public distancing from the invasion, as part of a broader personal and corporate reckoning. He remained connected to the ownership and board structure, but the operational leadership of the company changed hands at a moment of acute external pressure.

## Restructuring and rebirth: 2024

The solution that emerged over the following two years was a structural separation of the listed parent from the Russian operating business. In 2024, Yandex N.V. completed what was, in corporate-transaction terms, a substantial divestiture: the entire Russian operating business — the search engine, Yandex.Taxi, the food delivery platforms, the Russian cloud, and the adjacent domestic products — was sold to a consortium of Russian investors. The Netherlands-domiciled parent retained the international assets: the Nvidia GPU-cluster AI cloud business operating in European data centres, Toloka AI (a global human-data labelling platform), TripleTen (an online technology-education business), and Avride (the autonomous driving technology unit, formerly Yandex Self-Driving Group's international operations).

The parent was rebranded Nebius Group N.V. and continued to trade on NASDAQ under the new ticker NBIS. Volozh returned as chief executive to lead the refocused group, combining the institutional credibility of the original founder with the strategic mandate to rebuild the business around AI infrastructure.

The board was reconfigured to match the new strategic identity. Boynton remained as chairman and Ryan as an independent director — the two longest-serving outside directors, whose combined institutional knowledge of the company's founding, IPO, and decade of Russian market dominance gave the post-restructuring entity continuity and credibility with long-term shareholders. Around them, a set of newer directors was assembled to supply the capability set that a Netherlands-domiciled AI infrastructure company required.

## The post-restructuring board build

Ophir Nave joined as chief operating officer in May 2024 and was elected as an executive director at the August 2024 general meeting. His profile was calibrated precisely for the legal-architecture complexity of the restructuring: a Doctor of Juridical Science from Harvard Law School, a clerkship at the Israeli Supreme Court, a period at Wachtell Lipton Rosen & Katz in New York, and a lead partnership in the corporate and M&A practice at Arnon Tadmor-Levy in Israel. The assembly of a Netherlands-incorporated public company retaining international technology assets from a Russian operating entity while maintaining a NASDAQ listing is a feat of cross-border legal engineering; Nave's credential set is the explanation for how it was executed.

Elena Bunina joined as a non-executive director at the same August 2024 meeting. A mathematician with nearly seventy published research papers, she had previously served as general director of human resources and head of academic and educational services across the Yandex Group until April 2022. At Nebius she leads science and education, connecting directly to the TripleTen subsidiary and to the company's longer-term positioning in AI talent development.

Kira Radinsky joined as an independent non-executive director in 2024, bringing the board's most directly AI-domain-aligned credential: chief executive and chairwoman of Diagnostic Robotics, a US-based AI healthcare company, and founder of Mana Bio. Radinsky previously co-founded SalesPredict, an AI-powered sales analytics platform acquired by eBay in 2016, after which she served as eBay's director of data science and chief scientist for Israel. Her addition signalled the governance transformation from a Russia-focused internet conglomerate to an AI-infrastructure company requiring domain-expert oversight.

At the August 2025 annual general meeting, two further directors were elected. Arne Grimme, a partner at De Brauw Blackstone Westbroek and head of its corporate M&A practice, provided the Netherlands-domicile legal anchor the board required: Nebius is an N.V. incorporated under Dutch law, and Grimme's expertise in Dutch corporate governance and cross-border transactions addressed a governance gap. Matthew Weigand, a partner at Accel who had focused on enterprise software, financial technology, and security investments since 2013, joined concurrent with the close of Nebius's $700 million oversubscribed strategic equity placement — a financing that brought Accel, Nvidia, and Orbis Investments onto the shareholder register. Weigand had held observer rights ahead of his formal election; his board seat formalised the venture-capital governance stake in the AI-infrastructure thesis.

The resulting eight-director board at the snapshot date — Volozh as executive director and CEO, Nave as executive director and COO, Bunina as non-executive director, and five independent non-executive directors in Boynton, Ryan, Radinsky, Grimme, and Weigand — reads as a precise mapping of the strategic transformation: founder continuity plus legal architecture plus AI domain expertise plus Dutch corporate governance plus venture-co-investor oversight, all anchored by the two longest-serving figures who carry the institutional memory from 1990 through to 2026.

## The inflection and what it means

The operating numbers that emerged from the restructured entity by late 2025 established that the corporate transformation had been successfully converted into an AI-infrastructure business with genuine commercial velocity. Q4 2025 revenue reached $227.7 million, a 547 per cent year-on-year increase, with the core AI cloud segment growing at 802 per cent. Exit annual recurring revenue stood at $1.25 billion. The company held $3.7 billion of cash at year-end 2025, with $834 million of operating cash flow generated in Q4 alone — a prepayment signature from enterprise customers that provided working capital ahead of the capital expenditure cycle. Active data centre power reached 170 megawatts against more than 2 gigawatts contracted.

The FY2026 guidance that management issued in February 2026 was the most aggressive public commitment in the AI cloud peer set: revenue of $3.0 to $3.4 billion, capital expenditure of $16 to $20 billion, year-end ARR of $7 to $9 billion with more than half already contracted, and connected power of 800 megawatts to 1 gigawatt — a roughly five-fold increase from the year-end 2025 active base.

The thirty-six-year arc from a Moscow hardware-distribution company to a NASDAQ-listed AI cloud operator with a $16 to $20 billion annual capital expenditure programme is, at one level, an improbable straight line. At another, it is a precise illustration of what corporate restructuring can produce when the post-divestiture entity retains the institutional knowledge, the financial resources, and a founder willing to rebuild. The corporate history of Nebius Group is not prologue to the investment thesis — it is the investment thesis. The balance-sheet reconstitution, the board reconfiguration, and the Nvidia strategic relationship that formalised in the $700 million August 2025 placement are all outputs of a restructuring executed with enough speed and legal precision to catch the AI infrastructure cycle before the window narrowed. Whether the FY2026 capacity ramp can be delivered inside the guidance window is the operating question that dominates every subsequent chapter of this analysis; the corporate-history answer is that the organisational capability to attempt it was assembled more rapidly, and from more adverse starting conditions, than any comparable transformation in the current AI-infrastructure cohort.
